subject: correspondence between finite-sample estimates and predicted probabilities from occupancy models

messages.author: 70621566ba652451
messages.subject: correspondence between finite-sample estimates and predicted probabilities from occupancy models
parts:
Hello. I am working with some data on American Three-toed Woodpecker in spruce forest. I have fitted a model relating ATTW occupancy with 4 covariates. The model summary (from JAGS) is in the attached Excel file. I have plotted finite-sample occupancy estimates and predicted probabilities in relation to 4 covariates (see attached figure). Predicted probabilities (lines) along each covariate gradient were calculated while holding remaining covariates at their mean value, and finite-sample estimates (points with error bars) are the partially observed proportion of sampled points occupied within bins along each gradient. Error bars and lines represent 90% BCIs.

As you can see, the finite-sample estimates are not necessarily lining up with predicted probabilities (i.e., in plots B, C, and D), which has me scratching my head. I am wondering if others have seen this kind of mismatch, and if so is there cause for concern or an explanation for the mismatch?

In case it is helpful, all scripts for compiling data and fitting the model are posted on Github (https://github.com/qureshlatif/Julia-Kelly-Ch4).

Any insights or direction would be much appreciated!

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: correspondence between finite-sample estimates and predicted probabilities from occupancy models
parts:
Hi Quresh,

The mismatch is likely due to the nature of your multiple logistic regression for occupancy. The predicted probabilities are marginal effects for a given covariate with other covariates held at the observed population means, but the realized occupancy proportions involve sites with many different combinations of observed covariate values. I suppose binning them might wash out some of the differences but not all.

In case anyone is currently interested or becomes interested in the future, I did some further digging. First of all, I double-checked my code and am not seeing any errors in how finite-sample estimates are calculated. Second, I fit the same model to simulated data with known parameter values and the same covariate structure as field-collected data, and I checked how finite-sample estimates matched up with predicted probabilities. Attached plots show results for simulated data.

True values for sim 1 are Beta0 = 3, Beta.EarlInf = 10, p = 0.5, and all other parameters are set to 0.

True values for sim 1 are Beta0 = 0, Beta.EarlInf = 5, p = 0.5, and all other parameters are set to 0.

Credible intervals for all parameter estimates for models fitted to resulting data overlap corresponding true values.

Apparently, the mismatch between finite-sample estimates and predicted probabilities appears in plots for covariates with unsupported relationships with occupancy (and in truth no actual relationship, i.e., Beta.MidInf, Beta.snag, and Beta.QMD). So, it does not appear that this mismatch reflects any peculiarity of field-collected detection data, although it could very well be associated with the particular covariates and their inter-correlations included in the model.

I don't have any better explanation at this point than what Dan Linden has proposed, but I still don't feel particularly satisfied. I have been thinking of finite-sample estimates as (partially) observed values and therefore worth comparing to predicted probabilities in the same way that predictions from linear regression are often overlayed onto scatter plots of observed data to which the regression line was fitted. Apparently, finite-sample estimates are not completely analogous to observed data when it comes to displaying modeled covariate relationships in a plot, although I am not sure why this is the case.

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: correspondence between finite-sample estimates and predicted probabilities from occupancy models
parts:
Those simulation results make sense.  If the covariates do not have a strong relationship, you shouldn't expect the finite proportions to match the pattern very well.

One thing to remember here is that this is a logistic regression where the response is either 0 or 1, and given imperfect detection you're estimating which value is the true latent state for each site.  It would probably be better to plot the median values for latent occurrence instead of the predicted probabilities.  Then you can see the breakdown of covariate values across sites and which sites were predicted to be occupied on average (see Logistic regression).  This type of comparison between observed and predicted values will not mirror that of a standard linear regression, and even for a logistic regression it is a bit different because of the imperfect observations.
